read_scope.notes: Read the complete 22-page PDF, including references and Appendices A–G, through extracted text and rendered pages. Visually inspected every page, Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–11. Consulted frozen paper.tex and included results/table TeX to resolve wording and notation. Independently computed the supplied PDF SHA256. The abstract contains 155 whitespace-delimited words after normalizing TeX accents and punctuation. Extraction and rendering used an isolated /tmp/editorial_r20_b_ directory. No other reviews, previous versions, progress records or non-snapshot manuscript were inspected.

score_reasons.expression: Excellent, precise English with manageable sentences and unusually disciplined qualifications. Sections 4.1 and 5.4 explain contrasts and calibration in ordinary language before relying on symbols, while the conclusion accurately distinguishes name response from matching painter differences. There are only localized opportunities to make compact numerical displays and the historical mapping discussion easier to parse; no substantial prose repair is needed.
score_reasons.structure: The question, controlled prompt arms, feature representation, two primary scores and declared inferential family form a coherent progression. Section 5.1 establishes the primary result before Sections 5.2–5.5 explain common change, painter-pair unevenness, calibration and source sensitivity. Technical identities and older cohorts are appropriately optional appendices, and the main text supports its conclusions independently. The 22-page division is effective; remaining refinements concern small connections and labels rather than reorganization.
score_reasons.new_reader_understanding: The abstract stands alone within 155 words, the six clauses and finite reference target are clear, and the median-lightness example plus the no-distinction/exact/doubled examples make the metric interpretable. Table 2 and Section 5.1 distinguish positive alignment, total error and the no-contrast benchmark; Table 3 concretely explains the effect of averaging or calibrating. Figures and captions identify what is plotted and what it does not establish. Two small reader burdens remain: Table 10 encodes two different measures without labels in the header, and Appendix F.2 introduces prediction maps without immediately stating their input and output.
score_reasons.engagement: A consequential and concrete distinction drives the paper: a name can change an image without reproducing the labeled reference differences. Figure 1 gives a purposeful visual comparison, Figure 2 makes close painter positions inspectable through detail views, and Figure 3 exposes the weak Monet–Sisley response. The changing order under calibration and scene averaging is explained as a finding about the evaluation target rather than a model leaderboard. Results could connect back once more to the concrete lightness example, but the narrative already sustains attention without hype.

strengths: The introduction uses the Monet–Sisley example to explain why proximity to an artist collection does not establish correct differences between artists, and explicitly bounds the target to documented digital reproductions.

Section 4.1 gives both an observed lightness difference and three idealized generators with expected errors 1, 0 and 1. This is an effective bridge from an unfamiliar contrast metric to its numerical interpretation.
The 40-image Figure 1 is legible and has a precise selection/provenance caption; the controls make the intervention directly inspectable without implying matched historical compositions.

The primary result is stated with appropriate hierarchy: all models have positive aligned responses, FLUX has the lowest uncalibrated point estimate, only two adjusted model comparisons resolve, and no model is established to beat the no-distinction benchmark.

Table 3 and its surrounding text explain why both scalar calibration and scene averaging can change ordering, while clearly stating that images remain unchanged and overlapping folds do not establish superiority.
The source audit is reported transparently as an AI-coded retrospective sensitivity; Table 4 makes the changed comparison visible instead of burying it in an appendix.

findings.issue: Each painter column contains two numbers separated by a semicolon, but the header identifies only the painter. The two quantities have different interpretations and are identified only in the caption.
findings.reader_effect: A reader scanning across this dense table must repeatedly remember which number is an energy change and which is a variance ratio, increasing the chance of comparing unlike quantities.
findings.suggested_change: Add a compact second header line under each painter, such as “Δ energy ; variance ratio,” with short symbols defined in the caption if needed. Keep the existing six data rows and replace caption wording rather than adding a separate table or page.

findings.issue: The historical “Translation and scaling maps” and “named-mean prediction” are introduced without immediately identifying the map input and prediction target. The paragraph carefully distinguishes them from current calibration only at its end.
findings.reader_effect: An interested appendix reader has to reconstruct what is being predicted and how this earlier map differs from multiplying centered painter contrasts. This does not obstruct the standalone main narrative, but it weakens the optional explanation of the contrary transfer result.
findings.suggested_change: Replace the opening sentence with a sentence explicitly stating that the earlier maps predict named feature means from artist-free measurements using a fitted translation, with or without isotropic scaling, provided that wording matches the recorded map definition. Keep the existing held-out-scene qualification and final distinction from Table 3; no additional analysis or page is needed.

findings.location: Section 5.3, p. 8, in relation to Section 4.1, p. 5
findings.issue: The strong concrete median-lightness example is not revisited when the manuscript presents the all-feature Monet–Sisley result. The explanation consequently becomes entirely about aggregate numerical responses at the point where readers may want to connect the score to a measured image property.
findings.reader_effect: The pair result is understandable, but its connection to the earlier tangible example is left for the reader to make, slightly reducing continuity and engagement.
findings.suggested_change: Use a short cross-reference to the existing lightness example while introducing GPT Image 2’s .402 all-feature pair response, replacing part of the current opening sentence. Do not infer that lightness explains the full pair score or add new feature analyses.

summary: An excellent and self-contained account of a bounded digital-feature comparison. The central distinction, experimental arms, reference target, primary evidence and retrospective diagnostics are readily understandable. All figures and tables render cleanly. Remaining improvements are localized labels and explanatory connections, not substantial rewriting; no consequential claim-fidelity problem was identified within the editorial rubric.
